title: The angel of the mountains
hook: offered the two mountains brought down on his people, he refuses, hoping their children will worship Allah (Bukhari)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Addas and the grapes. Your line was: a bowl of grapes. Who did you bring food to, and what did you ask them? Day seven hundred fifty-three.

Revenge, offered from the sky. That's where today's story goes. A few days ago we heard him tell Aisha about the day he was turned away and walked in a daze until he reached Qarn al-Tha'alib. The same report in Sahih al-Bukhari doesn't stop there. He says that when he came to himself, he raised his head, and there was a cloud shading him. He looked, and in it was Jibril. Today: the angel of the mountains.
screen: `REVENGE FROM THE SKY.` → `A CLOUD OVERHEAD.` → `JIBRIL IN IT.`

segments.voice: Jibril calls down to him. In Bukhari's report he says, in effect: Allah has heard what your people said to you and how they answered you, and He has sent you the angel of the mountains, to order him as you wish. Then the angel of the mountains himself calls out, greets him, and says: if you wish, I will bring the two Akhshabs together over them. Commentators explain the two Akhshabs as the two mountains on either side of Mecca. Close them, and the people who mocked him are gone. Consider the timing. He has just lost his wife and his uncle. He has been refused, jeered, chased. He's alone. And now he's given the thing a wounded person might wish for: the power to make them pay, with heaven's permission. Here is his answer, in Bukhari. No. Rather, I hope that Allah will bring out from their descendants people who will worship Allah alone and associate nothing with Him. Look at what he chose to hope for. Not that they would apologize. Not even that they themselves would change. He looked past the people in front of him, to their children and grandchildren, people not yet born, and hoped for them. That is a long view, taken on the worst day. It also fits the du'a from two days ago, which complained of weakness but cursed no one. Muslims tell this story when they speak of the Prophet as a mercy, and Pickthall's Qur'an puts it this way in surah twenty-one: "We sent thee not save as a mercy for the peoples."
screen: `JIBRIL IN THE CLOUD.` · `THE TWO MOUNTAINS CAN CLOSE.` · `NO. I HOPE FOR THEIR CHILDREN.` · `A MERCY FOR THE PEOPLES.` · then, large: `HOPE FOR THEIR CHILDREN.`

segments.voice: The practice: refuse revenge. Sit, and let your breath settle. Bring to mind someone who has hurt you, not the worst person, just someone real. Notice what part of you would like to see them pay. Don't scold it. Just see it. Then, very simply, decline. Not forgive everything, not pretend it didn't happen. Just decline the revenge, for today. And then try his long view: think of someone connected to that person, a child, a friend, a future version of them, and wish that person well. If you pray, you can ask Allah for good for them. The bell holds the time.
The angel of the mountains. In Bukhari, offered the two mountains closed over the people who rejected him, he refuses, and hopes for their descendants instead. Today's word.
screen: `THE ANGEL OF THE MOUNTAINS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: hope for their children. Today, when you catch yourself wanting someone to pay, turn it into one good wish for someone who comes after them. Day seven hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: Muslims retell the angel of the mountains from Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim when speaking of the Prophet's mercy and restraint, and some read it alongside surah 21:107.

fork.setup: you've been rejected and chased. an angel offers to close two mountains over the people who did it. what do you say?
options: no; I hope their descendants will worship Allah.
wait until they've had one more chance.
fork.reveal: in Bukhari he refuses outright and hopes for their children's children.

original.note: Arabic: 'the two Akhshabs', the two mountains on either side of Mecca named in the hadith.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about an angel's power.
what it means: given the power to take revenge, he refused, and hoped for his enemies' children.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari 3231 and Muslim, from Aisha; the Akhshabs; read by some with 21:107, a mercy for the peoples.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 3231 (the cloud; Jibril; the angel of the mountains; the two Akhshabs; 'I hope that Allah will bring from their descendants people who worship Him alone')
Sahih Muslim 1795 (the same report from Aisha)

sources.quoted: We sent thee not save as a mercy for the peoples.

notes: Pickthall 21:107 quoted from memory ('We sent thee not save as a mercy for the peoples.'); confirm exact wording.
Bukhari 3231 and Muslim 1795 numbers cited from memory; confirm.
'The two mountains that stand on either side of Mecca' is the usual commentary gloss on al-Akhshabayn; confirm.
Bukhari places the day at al-Aqabah with Ibn Abd Yalil; commentators link it to the Ta'if journey. The script follows that link, as on day 750.
The index hook says the mountains would crush Ta'if; the Akhshabs are the mountains of Mecca, and the hadith says "them" (his people). The hook here says "his people". Confirm.
Practice distinguishes declining revenge from full forgiveness; confirm.
Editor pass: hook image changed from 'on a plate' (repeated yesterday's plate of grapes); the Akhshabs gloss now attributed to commentators, as the hadith doesn't define them.
